scenes.title: Open compensation and understand the fallback order

captions.text: In Workforce, open Compensation.
The page separates employee, role-default and department-default profiles.
Its help gives the estimate order: employee profile, then role
default, then department default.
It also says an approved payroll cost takes precedence.
This lesson creates one fictional department default so you can see its
settings and independent approval.
It does not set a real employee’s pay.
Select Add department default to open the form.

scenes.title: Set the effective period and hourly base

captions.text: Check the profile heading so you know which scope you are editing.
Set Effective to October first and Expires to November
thirtieth in this dated exercise.
Choose Hourly, use U S D, and enter a Base amount of twenty.
The form explains that the base is interpreted according to the pay basis.
Keep eight Hours per day and forty Hours per week.
The Regular hourly equivalent is an optional override; it stays blank here.
These are deliberately simple fictional values for checking
the software calculation.
Use the plus control in Pay components to add a row.
Each row has a Category, Name, Basis, Amount, Eligible pay codes
and a Per O T hour checkbox.
The example adds a named equipment differential with an amount of two
per hour for Regular and Standby.
Its overtime checkbox remains unchecked.
The panel explains that these components sit on top of the base.
Review the row as a separate contribution instead of putting
every cost into the base amount.

scenes.title: Add the employer cost and multipliers

captions.text: Use the plus control in Employer cost components for a separate fictional
overhead amount of five per hour, again limited to Regular and Standby.
Leave its optional Cap blank.
In Rate multipliers, the example sets Overtime to one point five, DoubleTime
to two, and Standby and Travel to one, using the J S O N structure shown.
Add a Source note that identifies this as a fictional software exercise.
These values are configuration examples, not prescribed rates for any department.

scenes.title: Save and read the loaded-day preview

captions.text: Select Save, then confirm the Saved message and the persisted inputs.
Scroll to Approval.
Resgrid previews a regular eight-hour day at two hundred sixteen dollars: one
hundred sixty in base pay, sixteen in pay components and forty in employer costs.
Those amounts match the configured twenty, two and five per hour.
The profile is still not approved.
The notice says unapproved profiles can price estimates but flag
their lines for review, and a rate change removes an approval.
Approve profile is a separate action from Save.
When the manager who made the latest change tries to approve
this example, Resgrid refuses.
The message says that it is the manager’s own pay or they made the latest change,
required_labels: You cannot approve this compensation profile: it is your own pay or you made its latest change. Another manager must approve it.

spoken_references.You cannot approve this compensation pro: manager’s own pay or they made the latest change

captions.text: and another manager must approve it.
The index still shows No in Approved.
Do not treat a saved profile or a calculated preview as approval.
Have a different authorized manager review the same profile
through their normal account.

scenes.title: Approve as a separate manager and verify the stored result

captions.text: The recording now uses a different, existing fictional
administrator, Kelly Severide.
The same department default is still not approved when that manager opens it.

spoken_references.Department default — not approved: department default is still not approved

captions.text: After reviewing the inputs and preview, select Approve profile.
The returned form shows the approval date, and the Compensation
index independently shows Yes.
That is the successful stored result.
The account switch uses normal sign-in; no permissions were changed and no
approval restriction was bypassed.

scenes.title: Apply the process to your own organization

captions.text: Use the same separation of preparation and review for search-and-rescue
teams, security companies, wildland contractors, industrial emergency
teams and community response services.
Community paramedicine, mental health response, fire and E M S
departments can all name components that fit their own organization.
Agree who maintains profiles, who independently approves them, and who
checks the resulting costing output.
Keep fictional exercises separate from operational compensation data.
